title: The Secret Skills of Master Teachers: Batching Busy (or Shallow) Work for the Sake of Deep Work ake-of-deep-work/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart takes up email as the archetype of shallow work, arguing that master teachers batch such busywork to protect deep work. He lays out why email is tricky: it comes from real people, is cheap to produce, is omnipresent on phones, and yet never builds expertise or mastery. Drawing on Cal Newport's distinction, he treats almost all email as necessary but low in long-term value. His rules are only handling each message once, removing email from his phone, unsubscribing from perpetual don't-reads, and scheduling two or three 20-minute sessions per day. He names batching as the skill he suspects most master teachers share and wants to develop further.
points: Email is human, cheap, omnipresent, and non-expert-building, which explains why instinct leads to too much of it.
Following Cal Newport, nearly all email is shallow work: often necessary, but not where students' long-term flourishing is figured out.
Deleting the mail app from his phone made the only-handle-it-once rule practical and improved his home life.
Unsubscribing from newsletters he repeatedly auto-archives removes a recurring decision.
Batching email into two or three focused 20-minute sessions is the central practice and a skill he wants to deepen.
quotes: Treated instinctively, emails are omnipresent. Where there is an Internet connection, there is the potential for email. Smartphones come with email apps already installed. So email is always there, always promising us dopamine if we open the app and find a new message, always offering us a chance to “get caught up” by pulling out our devices and getting a few emails answered. Our instincts will always lead us to too much email time.
Email, despite its humanity and its omnipresence, doesn't produce expertise or mastery. That's the point most relevant to today's post.

Perhaps 99.5% of our emails are what the eminently productive (and work-life balancing) Georgetown professor Cal Newport would define as “shallow work.” This isn't to say that email is bad — honestly, I love corresponding with people — it's just that it's not super great from a long-term perspective. Many of our emails need to be done, but they're unlikely to produce long-term value or help us solve the problems that we're wrestling with.
To put it another way, then, email is busy work — it's always got something for us to do. And yet, it won't give us the kinds of breakthroughs that sustained, hard work will.

For the longest time, I was an addict to pulling out my phone and checking my email. But I almost never responded to emails on my phone because it's cumbersome and I like to write in complete sentences. So then I just deleted the mail app from my phone. This makes OHIO a lot easier.
I schedule two or three 20-minute chunks per day, and during those two or three sessions, I'm intensely focused.
That last bit — batching — is a skill that I suspect most master teachers have. So, it's one I'd like to further develop.
